newsitem.title: USA: Corn prices at two-year low as crop flourishes.
newsitem.headline: Corn prices at two-year low as crop flourishes.

text.p: Corn prices fell to their lowest level in more than two years on Wednesday as crop-growing weather in the U.S. Midwest turned nearly ideal.
Warm temperatures plus showers and high humidities enhanced crop production prospects, traders said.
"We continue to make new lows. There's very, very good weather," said Tom Levis, Prudential Securities grain analyst.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture earlier this week said 67 percent of the crop was in good or excellent condition, up from 60 percent at the same point last year when production totalled 9.3 billion bushels, the third largest ever.
Traders said this week's weather had further improved the condition of the crop, which could challenge the 1994 record of 10.1 billion.
The bulk of U.S. corn is harvested in October. Iowa and Illinois are the leading corn producing states.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for July delivery touched a low of $2.55-3/4 a bushel, the lowest level for the nearby contract since May 1995. July closed four cents down on the day at $2.56-1/4.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, feeder cattle futures closed higher, boosted by the falling cost of key feed ingredients such as corn.
Concern about tightness in the supply of feeder cattle this fall was also supportive.

"You just continue to hear that it is hard to find feeders for this fall because the greatest majority of them are contracted already, so the cash (feeder) market is going to be rather tight," Dean Witter analyst Dale Benson said.
Feeder cattle for August delivery closed 0.300 cent per pound higher at 78.600 cents.
The CME's index of feeder cattle prices in the cash market was up 0.59 cent at 77.56 cents per pound, the highest since August 18, 1994.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil futures ended higher as OPEC members vowed to adhere to output quotas after the group agreed to roll over their 25.03 million barrel per day production ceiling.

"The tone of the rollover is what everyone has focused on," said Michael Busby, a trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York. "All the members actually admitted there is a quota-busting problem, and they have agreed to do something about it."
August crude settled 49 cents higher at $19.52 a barrel. July gasoline finished up 1.29 cents a gallon at 56.97 cents while July heating oil ended 1.42 cents higher at 52.99 cents a gallon.
At a summer meeting in Vienna, oil ministers from the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries agreed to roll over their self-imposed production ceiling for six months starting July 1.

Chronic quota violations have lifted OPEC output two million barrels above the group's self-imposed 25.03 million barrel per day ceiling, but Saudi oil minister Ali bin Ibrahim al-Naimi said OPEC had a high level of commitment toward keeping output allocations.
"We have a very high level of commitment...one hundred percent," he told reporters.

Meanwhile, Iran's oil minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh said the issue of output quota compliance by OPEC members was solved. The statement followed a meeting of the oil ministers of Iran, Saudia Arabia and Venezuela about quota compliance. A Gulf source said Venezuela admitted to 800,000 barrels per day of overproduction during the OPEC meeting.

"What happens tomorrow will depend on how Venezuela responds to the statements by other members today," Busby said. OPEC is expected to resume its meeting early Thursday morning, and dealers expect Venezuela's oil minister Erwin Arrieta to make a statement about the meeting afterwards.
